title: Medication vs. Therapy: How to Decide (Or Do Both)
description: Should you try medication, therapy, or both? What research shows about treatment effectiveness, and how to make the right choice for your situation.

content.text: It's one of the first decisions in mental health treatment: pills, talk therapy, or both? Here's what the evidence actually shows.
Therapy and medication are equally effective for mild-moderate depression. Combination is slightly better than either alone.
Combination treatment (medication + therapy) is significantly more effective than either alone. Medication may be necessary to create enough relief to engage in therapy.
CBT is as effective as medication, with longer-lasting effects. Combination is often recommended for moderate-severe cases.
Therapy (especially CBT) has longer-lasting effects after stopping treatment. Medication benefits often disappear when you stop taking it. This favors including therapy in your treatment.

items: Can make therapy possible when symptoms are severe
Easy to access (any doctor can prescribe)
Addresses root causes, not just symptoms
Works for people who don't respond to meds
Helps with issues beyond diagnosis (relationships, meaning)
Severe symptoms interfering with daily function
Symptoms that make therapy difficult to engage in
For conditions that respond well to meds (bipolar, ADHD)
When learning skills is the goal
For conditions that respond best to therapy (OCD, PTSD)

content.text: For moderate-to-severe depression and anxiety, combination treatment is more effective than either alone. The whole is greater than the sum of its parts.
Medication can lift you enough to engage in therapy. Therapy can help you eventually taper off medication. They work synergistically.

There's no universal right answer. For mild-moderate symptoms, either can work—choose based on your preferences and access. For severe symptoms, combination is usually best. Whatever you choose, give it a real chance before switching approaches.
